_comment: The Amber Mile. A fixed ten-stop walk round the Main Town of Gdansk. Unlike the London tour there is no topic picking: one route, one order, everybody walks the same thing. Nothing is dated and nothing is shared, so any number of people can walk it at once, independently, at any time.
name: The Amber Mile

intro.lead: Ten stops round the old centre of Gdansk.
intro.body:
About a mile of walking and an hour if you do not stop for beer. Seven stops ask you a question you can only answer by looking at the thing in front of you. Three just need you to be standing in the right place.

Everything is outdoors and free. You never have to go into a museum.
intro.start: Start at the Upland Gate, the Brama Wyzynna, at the western end of the old town on Waly Jagiellonskie. It is the low stone gate with three carved shields on it, a few minutes from the main station.

topics.name: Merchants and Kings
topics.blurb: A port that got rich on other people's grain, and the foreigners who came for a cut.

topics.name: Gold, Amber and Water
topics.blurb: Why this city is the colour it is.

topics.name: Burnt and Rebuilt
topics.blurb: Almost none of this is old. All of it is real.

stops.title: The Upland Gate
stops.where: Brama Wyzynna, Waly Jagiellonskie, at the western end of the old town

question.ask: Three carved shields run across the front of the gate, and each one is held up by a pair of animals. One of those pairs has a single horn in the middle of its forehead. What are they?
question.hint: Look at the shield on the left as you face the gate. The two beasts holding it are not horses.

stops.look:
Stand back far enough to see the whole front of the gate.

There are three shields in a row. Each one is held up by a pair of creatures.

Look at all three pairs before you answer. They are not the same animal.
stops.after:
Left to right, those are the arms of Royal Prussia held by unicorns, Poland held by angels, and Gdansk held by lions. Three rulers on one wall, in the order that mattered to whoever paid for the carving.

This is the start of the Royal Route. When a Polish king came to Gdansk he came in through this gate and walked the way you are about to walk, straight down to the river. The city put on a show along it, and the show is still standing.

The gate went up between 1574 and 1588, and the shields were added in 1586.

The two crosses on the Gdansk shield turn up everywhere once you have seen them. Manhole covers, lamp posts, bins. Start counting.

stops.title: The Golden Gate
stops.where: Zlota Brama, at the top of ulica Dluga
stops.directions:
Face the old town with the Upland Gate behind you and walk straight ahead, east, about two hundred metres.

You pass a squat round brick tower on your left. That is the old Prison Tower.

Keep going through the short passage. The next gate, pale stone with statues standing on the roofline, is the Golden Gate.

question.ask: Stand on the far side and look up at the roofline. How many figures are standing along the top?
question.hint: They are spaced along the parapet, one above each column.

stops.look:
Walk through and turn round so the gate is in front of you and the long street is at your back.

Look at the very top, along the roofline.

There are figures up there. Count them.
stops.after:
Four, and they are virtues. On this side, Peace, Liberty, Wealth and Fame. Walk round to the other side and there are four more: Concord, Justice, Piety and Prudence.

The split is the point. Facing out at the world, the city advertised what it had. Facing in at its own citizens, it listed what it expected of them.

The gate was built in 1612 by Abraham van den Blocke, a Flemish architect, which tells you where Gdansk was looking. Not east and not south. Across the sea, at Amsterdam and Antwerp.

Almost every good building on this walk was designed by a Dutchman or a Fleming.

stops.title: The Main Town Hall
stops.where: Ratusz Glownego Miasta, on the right hand side where ulica Dluga opens out
stops.directions:
Go through the Golden Gate and keep walking east along ulica Dluga, the wide street with the tall painted houses down both sides.

Stay on it for about two hundred and fifty metres.

The Town Hall is the tall building on your right with the one very high spire. Stand back on the left hand side of the street so you can see the top of it.

question.ask: There is a small gilded figure on the very top of the spire, above everything else. Is he a king, a saint, or a sailor?
question.hint: He is holding something in each hand, and one of them is not a tool.

stops.look:
Look up. Keep going up, past the clock, past the gallery, to the very tip.

There is a small gold figure standing on the top.

He is about eighty metres above your head, so squint.
stops.after:
A king. Sigismund II Augustus, put up there in 1561, and gilded so that he would be the brightest thing in the city.

Now the part worth knowing. In March 1945 the Soviet army shelled and burned this city centre for days, and about ninety per cent of the Main Town was destroyed. Over a thousand buildings. This tower burned and the spire came down.

So the king above you is a copy, on a rebuilt tower, on a street that was rubble to the height of a person.

Look down the street at the houses. Almost every one of them is younger than the Beatles. They were rebuilt from photographs, paintings and the memories of people who had lived in them, and the work went on into the nineteen sixties.

It is not a fake. It is a city that was killed and then copied back out by hand.
stops.after_spoken:
A king. Sigismund the Second Augustus, put up there in fifteen sixty-one, and gilded so that he would be the brightest thing in the city.

Now the part worth knowing. In March nineteen forty-five the Soviet army shelled and burned this city centre for days, and about ninety per cent of the Main Town was destroyed. Over a thousand buildings. This tower burned and the spire came down.

stops.title: Neptune's Fountain
stops.where: Fontanna Neptuna, in Dlugi Targ just past the Town Hall
stops.directions:
Carry on east for another sixty metres.

The street opens out into a wide square. This is Dlugi Targ, the Long Market.

The fountain is straight ahead of you behind an iron railing, with a dark green figure standing on top.

question.ask: Neptune is holding a long fork. How many points are on the end of it?
question.hint: It is the standard sea god issue. Count the prongs.

stops.look:
Get close to the railing and look up at him.

He is bronze, gone green, and he is looking down at the water with his fork lowered.

Count the points on the end of it.
stops.after:
Three. It is a trident, and there is a story attached to it.

Gdansk merchants used to throw coins into this fountain. Neptune got sick of it, struck the water with the trident, and shattered the gold into thousands of tiny flakes.

That is the city's own explanation for Goldwasser, the herbal liqueur that has been made here since the sixteenth century with real gold leaf floating in it. Twenty-two carat. You can buy a bottle two minutes from where you are standing and the flakes are still in there.

The fountain went up between 1606 and 1633 and it was the first monumental fountain in Poland.

And he is facing the right way. He is turned towards the Artus Court behind him, not out at the square, because the merchants in that building were the ones who paid for him.

stops.title: Artus Court
stops.where: Dwor Artusa, the tall building directly behind Neptune
stops.directions:
Turn away from the middle of the square and face north.

The building immediately behind the fountain, with the four tall arched windows and the stepped gable above them, is Artus Court.

It is about twenty metres. Go and stand at the foot of its steps.

gate.prompt: Stand at the front of Artus Court, right behind the fountain.

stops.look:
Stand facing the front of it and look at the four big arched windows.

This was not a church, a palace or a town hall.

It was a club.
stops.after:
It is named after King Arthur. Yours.

The merchants who met here wanted to think of themselves as knights round a round table, dealing fairly and behaving well. The fashion for naming a merchants' hall after Arthur started in England, spread across the North Sea, and washed up here. The building is recorded as curia regis Artus, the court of King Arthur, in 1357.

And there is a better British connection than the name.

By the seventeenth century somewhere near eighteen hundred Scots were living in Gdansk, about one person in forty. There were so many that two districts of this city are still called Stare Szkoty and Nowe Szkoty. Old Scotland and New Scotland.

One of them, a merchant called William Forbes, made a fortune here and went home to Aberdeenshire with it. He built Craigievar Castle, the pink tower house on the Scottish shortbread tins. His nickname was Danzig Willie.

So a castle in Aberdeenshire was paid for out of this square.

stops.title: The Golden House
stops.where: Zlota Kamienica, Dlugi Targ 41, on the same side as Artus Court
stops.directions:
Keep going east along the same side of Dlugi Targ, away from the Town Hall, for about forty metres.

You want number 41, four doors along.

You will know it when you see it. The whole front is covered in carving, and the carving is not stone coloured.

question.ask: The carvings and lettering all over the front of this house are picked out in one colour, and it is the colour the house is named after. What is it?
question.hint: It is in the name of the building.

stops.look:
Stand across the street so you can see the whole front at once.

Every band of carving is picked out. There are busts of rulers, battle scenes, and a line of figures above them.

Look at what colour it has all been finished in.
stops.after:
Gold, and it is real gilding, not paint.

The house was built between 1609 and 1618 for a mayor named Johann Speymann, and the busts along it are rulers he wanted to be associated with, including Zygmunt III Waza and Wladyslaw Jagiello. The single figure balanced on the very top is Fortune.

Here is why it belongs with the Town Hall. In 1945 this house burned like everything else, and what was left standing was the front wall on its own, scorched and leaning, three storeys of it, about to fall into the street.

They did not knock it down. They propped it up and rebuilt the house behind it, using the surviving wall as the pattern. The regilding was still being finished in 1955.

So of everything on this square, this face is one of the few that genuinely came through. Everything behind it is new.

stops.title: The Green Gate
stops.where: Brama Zielona, the big brick building closing the end of Dlugi Targ
stops.directions:
Carry on east to the end of Dlugi Targ, about a hundred and twenty metres.

The wide brick building blocking the whole end of the square, with the arched passages cut through it, is the Green Gate.

Stand in front of it, on the square side.

gate.prompt: Get to the front of the Green Gate at the far end of the Long Market.

stops.look:
Look at the size of it, and then at what it is made of.

It is not a gate in the way the last two were. It has rooms, and windows, and chimneys.

It is a building with holes punched through it.
stops.after:
It is a palace, and no king would live in it.

It was built in the 1560s as an official residence for Polish kings when they came to Gdansk. The city spent a fortune on it and modelled it on the town hall in Antwerp.

The kings took one look and stayed somewhere else. It was on the main square, on the road to the river, next to the market, and it was far too noisy. As a royal residence it was used essentially once.

Walk through it. On the other side is the Motlawa, and that river is the entire reason for this city. Grain came down the Vistula from half of Poland, was stored in the warehouses on the far bank, and went out to Amsterdam, to Antwerp and to England.

Gdansk did not grow the grain. It just stood at the point where the river met the sea and charged everybody.

stops.title: The Crane
stops.where: Zuraw, on the waterfront path north of the Green Gate
stops.directions:
Walk through one of the arches of the Green Gate and out to the river.

Turn left and follow the waterfront path, Dlugie Pobrzeze, north for about two hundred and fifty metres. The river stays on your right the whole way.

You pass a run of brick gateways on your left, one at the end of each street. Do not bother counting them, just keep going north.

The Crane is the enormous wooden housing slung between two brick towers and leaning out over the water. You will not walk past it by accident.

question.ask: The big wooden crane housing is held up between brick towers. How many towers are there?
question.hint: One either side of the timber.

stops.look:
Stand back along the quay so you can see the whole thing side on.

A great slab of timber leans out over the water, sitting between towers of brick.

Count the brick towers.
stops.after:
Two, and the timber between them is the machine.

This was built between 1442 and 1444 and it was the biggest working crane in medieval Europe. It could lift two tonnes to a height of twenty-seven metres, and if you coupled both pairs of wheels together, four tonnes to eleven.

There was no engine. Inside those timbers are enormous wooden treadwheels, and the power was men walking inside them, like hamsters. Several at a time, for hours.

It did two jobs. It loaded cargo, and it stepped masts into ships, which is a thing almost nothing else in Europe could do at that size.

It burned in 1945 along with everything else, and what you are looking at was rebuilt in the fifties and sixties. The brick towers are largely original. The wooden part is not.

One thing that will not match the older photographs. Until recently the timber was almost black. A three year restoration finished in 2024 and the wood came back a much lighter brown, which is far closer to how it looked when it was still lifting things.

stops.title: Ulica Mariacka
stops.where: The street running west from the river through Brama Mariacka
stops.directions:
Turn round and walk back south along the waterfront, the way you came, about a hundred and fifty metres.

You are looking for a gateway on your right with a pointed roof and a small tower, signed Brama Mariacka. Read the signs rather than counting the gates, because there are more of them than you expect. If you get back to the Green Gate you have gone too far.

Go through it, away from the river. You are now at the bottom of ulica Mariacka. Walk a little way up it and stop.

gate.prompt: Get onto Mariacka itself, in among the stone terraces.

stops.look:
Stand in the middle of the street and look at the fronts of the houses.

Nobody's front door is at street level. Every house has a raised stone platform in front of it, with steps up and an iron rail round it.

Now look at the stone spouts sticking out from them.
stops.after:
Those platforms are przedproza, and they are a Gdansk speciality.

The ground here is low and wet, so the houses were built up above the street. The space that left in front became a sort of outdoor room where you sat, did business and greeted people, half in the house and half in the street.

The spouts are rzygacze, which is a blunter word in Polish than gargoyle is in English. They throw the roof water out over the pavement, and every one is carved differently. Dragons, fish, faces. If it rains hard, do not stand under one.

One of them, between numbers 6 and 7, has a name. Pomuchel, which is Kashubian for a Baltic cod.

And look in the windows. Nearly every shop on this street sells one thing, and it is the reason Gdansk calls itself the amber capital of the world. It washes up on the beaches a few miles from here, and it is pine resin that has been sitting around for forty million years.

stops.title: St Mary's
stops.where: Bazylika Mariacka, filling the west end of Mariacka
stops.directions:
Walk west up Mariacka, away from the river, about a hundred metres to the end.

The street runs straight at the church, which is the point.

Stop where the street ends and the building starts, and get your back against something so you can look up.

question.ask: This is one of the biggest churches in the world of its kind. What is it built out of?
question.hint: Get close and look at the wall. It is not stone.

stops.look:
Look at the size of it first, then walk up and put your hand flat on the wall.

All the great cathedrals you can name are made of cut stone.

This one is not.
stops.after:
Brick. It is the largest brick church in the world, and depending on how you measure, one of the largest churches of any kind.

It is a hundred and five metres long and the inside will hold something like twenty thousand people. There is no stone here because there is no stone here. Northern Poland is flat, wet and made of clay, so the whole region built in brick and got very good at it.

It took about a hundred and sixty years to finish, from 1379 to 1502.

In 1945 the roof and the vaults burned and much of the inside was destroyed. The walls held. It was patched, then properly rebuilt, and the work went on for decades.

That is the last thing worth taking away from this walk.

The Town Hall, the Golden House, the Crane and this church all burned in the same few weeks of one spring. Every one of them was put back by hand. The people who did it decided that a careful copy of the truth was better than an honest hole in the ground.

outro:
That is the ten.

If you have any walking left, the shipyard is twenty minutes north of here. That is where the strikes of 1980 started, and where the thing that eventually pulled down the Berlin Wall got going. It is a different walk and it deserves its own hour.
